name: Recording and transcribing speech
summary: Keeping the audio is only the start. A recording you can work with has to let you check the words, find the moment you need and pass the material on.
lead:
A voice recorder has several different finish lines. An interview needs the whole conversation, a meeting needs agreements that have been checked, work on a book needs the chapter continued. A month later a single exact phrase may be all that is wanted.

These jobs all begin with the record button, but the work they take after it differs. Let us look at how not to lose the audio, how to turn it into material you can check, and how to find what you need in the archive you have built up.

audiencesArt.alt: Different jobs in the “Voice recording and transcription” category.

audiences.title: Recording a long meeting or lecture
audiences.body: A long session calls for a limit that is clear in advance and a recording state you can see. A person can put the phone away and focus on the conversation, but they have to know what was saved once it ends.

audiences.title: Preparing a text from a conversation
audiences.body: Working with a conversation depends on words and speakers you can check. The editing has to be saved together with the link to the source audio, so that a disputed phrase can be returned to.

audiences.title: Building up a personal voice archive
audiences.body: Short notes pile up into a collection. A recording from the watch has to turn up somewhere reachable, and an old thought has to be findable by a name that makes sense and shareable in the format you need.

sections.title: First keep all the audio you need
sections.intro: A short trial tests the start. A long recording, an interruption and a playback test the complete scenario.

observations.title: Knowing which part of the conversation was saved
passages: Background recording lets you put the phone away with the screen off and focus on the conversation. The positive review below describes exactly that convenient foundation. But a successful start does not yet mean the material will survive until the next time you need it.

Whether the file is reachable is also tested after you stop: when renaming, moving and reopening it. The author of the next review praises background recording but reports that the renamed files vanished. Good work from the microphone did not save the result here; what has been saved has to stay reachable whatever it is called.

Another risk is ending up with only part of a long conversation without noticing. Before you start you need to see the limit on a single recording; afterwards, the actual duration and any cutoff. Notes from the first thirty minutes can look complete even though the rest of the meeting never made it in. The audio and the readiness of its transcript are worth showing separately.

quotes.text: Free version has few features, but sufficient and well selected from the entire set. Easy to use. Does not crash. Very nice that it operates in the background.

I had several recordings that I changed the name to and all of them are gone. Only the ones named 'Recorder' with incrementing numbers stayed. The app is nice and can record even when changing apps or when the screen shuts off.

I bought this app specifically to record phone calls due to a restraining order on the first attempt to use it. It only recorded 30 minutes of an hour and a half phone call rendering it completely useless.

art.alt: Illustration for the theme “Knowing which part of the conversation was saved”.

placements.title: Knowing which part of the conversation was saved

observations.title: Knowing in advance how the conversation gets recorded
passages: Recording the microphone and recording a call are different actions. In the reviews cited here, a call means merging the calls while the other person is already waiting for an answer. It helps to show the whole supported method in advance and to let people try it, rather than leaving the extra steps for the moment of an important conversation.

Even a few seconds of connecting change the opening of a conversation. A person needs to understand at what point the audio actually started being saved and what part of the conversation may have been left before that point. A separate connection status is more useful than an icon that looks the same before a recording and during it.

Beeps also become part of the conversation: in the review below the other person asks about them outright. Features like that should be explained before use. This evidence concerns specific ways of recording; you cannot conclude from it that every app on every device starts the same way.

quotes.text: My problem is the steps and time it takes to start recording. The 5 steps can take up to 10 seconds to begin recording. 1 Answer call 2 Go to Home Screen 3 Open the app 4 Tap record 5 Tap merge call. In the meantime the call has been answered and the person on the other line is expecting a response.
The initial merge of TapeACall into the call took several seconds and during that time, there was a slight pause in the conversation.

It seems all call recording apps require you to merge calls, which isn't ideal at all.. after merging the call you'll hear a loud beep on both parties phones, literally had a lawyer stop and say 'what was that..' however compared to the rest of the apps this one does the job as far as recording.

placements.title: Knowing in advance how the conversation gets recorded
placements.body: After the recording a separate job remains: keep an accessible original and tell its working copies apart. It matters whatever way you connected to the conversation.

observations.title: Checking the speech and editing reversibly
passages: Audio quality comes down to whether the speech you need can be made out in a particular setting. The reviewer below got a good result on speakerphone. A short listen before a long session helps you tell whether the position chosen for the phone and the mode suit it.

With a strong background the recording can exist and still not let you hear the important words. Processing is useful if it improves intelligibility rather than simply making the sound pleasant. Afterwards it is worth comparing the disputed fragment with the original: a smoothed sound does not yet confirm that the speech is accurate.

That kind of check needs a saved original and reversible editing. Undoing the last action is different from reverting to the very beginning: the latter destroys the work that went well too. The next review shows why step-by-step undo matters even in a voice recorder’s small editor.

quotes.text: The quality of the voice recording was exceptionally good, and it was good even though I was sharing my iPhone on speaker with another participant in the call.
Too much background static. Not clear hard to hear the voices!

Edit: HUGE flaw, I actually tried to use it. It's extremely frustrating because they don't have an 'undo' they have a 'revert to original' and no way to save the progress. Dude… why don't you have an undo?

art.alt: Illustration for the theme “Checking the speech and editing reversibly”.

sections.title: Turning the transcript into checked material
sections.intro: Automatic text is useful as a draft, as long as every important phrase can be checked and corrected.

observations.title: Correcting a word and a speaker’s name
passages: Fast text is convenient for a first pass through a conversation, but a single error can change an important detail. Labeling the speakers adds another job: the same voice has to keep a stable name, and a correction must not have to be typed again for every line.

It helps to tie the words and the speaker labels to the source audio. A doubtful spot can be listened to, a name clarified, the corrected result saved. Then the transcription becomes working material: its value lies in how easy it is to check and to use further, not in having to trust every line at once.

A dictionary of your own names and terms can cut down on repeated corrections, but its usefulness has to be tested on the audience’s real recordings. The way a correction is made matters just as much: renaming one speaker across the whole conversation, fixing a term and saving the confirmed version separately from a new automatic draft.

quotes.text: I found the following features very helpful 1. Transcribes m4a audio files very accurately and very fast! 2. It transcribes a 30min audio file in matter of minutes 3. It very accurately identifies different speakers & assigns speech text to them.

Like almost all generative AI products, this one isn't ready for prime time yet. There are some things it does relatively well, like transcribing speech to text. That part of it is maybe 80% there. But that 20% where it doesn't transcribe accurately is important, because it means you'll constantly have to review everything.

Not that great at identifying names of speakers. My hope is that it would identify a voice and give it a speaker number, but you have to go in and label every speaker even when it's the same person and you've already given them a label.

placements.title: Correcting a word and a speaker’s name

observations.title: Keeping the agreements that were checked
passages: Automatic notes mean you are less distracted by your own note-taking during a meeting. The benefit in the first review is simple: a person listens to the conversation and comes back to the notes afterwards. But the finished text still has to be checked.

After a few meetings the value shifts to search: you can recall where a question was discussed and open the original conversation. At the same time an option that was discussed cannot automatically be treated as a decision that was made. It helps to tie an item in the notes to the phrase it rests on and to allow the wording to be refined.

That proofreading is pointless if the edits vanish after the “done” button. The checked version has to be saved separately from a new automatic draft. Before passing the document on, a person has to see their own refinements, not the original text quietly restored.

quotes.text: In the past I was sitting in a meeting and focusing on my notes, not listening to the actual meeting. I dont multi-task. Now I can sit in a meeting, focus on whats being said and when it's over - the notes are there.

I absolutely love Otter.ai! It has completely changed the way I take notes and keep track of meetings. The transcription is fast, accurate, and saves me so much time. I also love the summaries and how easy it is to search through past conversations.
Everything is great except when I edit the summary of the recording (which is sometimes rigorous) it does not save when I click 'done'. Very frustrating that it cannot be edited effectively.

art.alt: Illustration for the theme “Keeping the agreements you have checked”.

placements.title: Keeping the agreements that were checked

observations.title: Getting back to a quote in one jump
passages: A time marker shortens the path from the text to the phrase you heard. Even an imperfect transcript can be useful as an index: the reader spots a doubtful word and opens the matching audio instead of hunting for it across the whole recording.

Proofreading needs a small margin of context. Resuming a few seconds earlier lets you hear the beginning of a line again and check the exact quote. That simple action can be more useful than one more automatically generated summary.

The link to time matters after export too. If images and text lose their placement, the recipient sees different material from the editor. An interviewer needs a fragment with the speaker, the time and a comment; the final file is worth checking against those links, not only for the presence of text.

quotes.text: Not very accurate. I like the time stamps though.

I wish there was an option to start playback 5 seconds previous when pausing a recording that you're listening to. This would really help when you're transcribing and you need to make sure the quote is exactly right.

Cannot export pictures and text together in one file with pictures in the correct time stamp and location - which is how it appears in the app. This makes it very difficult for use for serious user: I don't get what I see in the app.

placements.title: Getting back to a quote in one jump
placements.body: A book author’s next step is different: not picking a quote out of an interview, but continuing a text already begun with a new dictation. One transcript does not cover both scenarios.

sections.title: Finding a recording and using it again
sections.intro: Over time the value shifts to search, to names that hold and to being able to take your own archive away.

observations.title: Getting a thought from the watch to the phone
passages: Recording a thought from your wrist is convenient when you do not want to get the phone out. After that the note has to end up somewhere you can listen to it and use it. In the positive review that path starts with a spontaneous thought and ends with a note or an audio message.

Unpredictable transfer leaves a doubt: is the job over once the recording stops? It helps to show “saved on the watch” and “a copy on the phone” separately, and to keep the original file until the transfer is confirmed. Those states matter more than one more list of recent notes.

If the automatic transfer did not finish, a person has to understand how to repeat it or get the file by hand. After the transfer the old name and time help you recognize the note. Otherwise you end up hunting for one piece of audio across two devices and guessing which of several similar cards holds the thought you want.

quotes.text: This app is so practical for saving mental notes or sending long audio messages to friends. The most amazing option is that I can do it by my apple watch.
What the heck is going on with the Apple Watch syncing… Recordings from the watch go on to the phone whenever they feel like it… If ever at all!
It's nice that this app has a feature to record on my watch, but I can't figure out how to transfer it to my phone, which makes the watch app kind of useless.

art.alt: Illustration for the theme “Getting a thought from the watch to the phone”.

observations.title: Finding the phrase you need months later
passages: A single recording is useful as long as it can be found. As the archive grows, search, names and folders become part of the main work rather than decoration for a collection. In the review below good audio and convenient sharing sit next to a hard time finding the files themselves.

A name is one way of remembering the content without listening again. If it does not stick, the user loses the result of their own labeling. Renaming has to hold at the next opening and the next transfer; only then is it worth adding search across recognized words with a jump to the original minute.

It matters to be able to take the whole accumulated archive away. Exporting one file at a time is fine for a one-off send, but it becomes heavy work for a collection. For family voices what is especially valuable is ordinary files you can listen to, with names and dates preserved — even if there is a more sophisticated search inside the app.

quotes.text: I've made many recordings with this app over the years. The clarity and ability to share sound files is great, but locating files is a difficult task.

After recording, I changed the file name but it didn't remain there. It's disappeared and I should do that work again to have file name changed. Sometimes I should repeat that boring process even several times. What's the problem?
They removed feature to start recording before calling and to DL your calls you have to go through one by one to transfer. No mass exodus feature.

placements.title: Finding the phrase you need months later

conclusion.title: Keep it first, shorten it later
conclusion.body:
The first priority here is complete audio you can reach: a clear duration, survival after renaming and the ability to get a separate copy. Without that, even an accurate transcript and convenient notes rest on material that may disappear or turn out to be incomplete. The next priority is editing you can verify: going from a word to the audio, correcting a speaker and not losing the change you made.

After that it is worth choosing one complete scenario. An interviewer needs quotes, an author needs the chapter continued, a family needs an archive of voices that makes sense. These jobs do not call for the same set of features. They are better tested against a finished result outside the app than combined under one “process the recording” button.
